questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main reframing of meetings?
choices: Meetings are costly claims on shared attention that should be earned
Meetings are harmless because they look organized
Meetings should always happen whenever people feel uncertain

explanation.gentle: The chapter treats meetings as expensive uses of shared time.
explanation.direct: Meetings must justify their live claim on attention.
explanation.competitive: The invite is an invoice, not a decoration.

choices: Because they claim multiple calendars and attention blocks at once
Because rooms are always expensive to rent
Because meetings are longer than writing by law

explanation.gentle: The cost multiplies across everyone in the room.
explanation.direct: Shared attention is the key unit of cost here.
explanation.competitive: One hour times many people stops being small fast.

questions.prompt: What makes weak meetings survive socially?
choices: Formal scheduling can make vague meetings look justified even when they are not
Every meeting has obvious value the moment it is booked
People can always tell in advance which meetings will be excellent

explanation.gentle: The calendar can make weak meetings look more necessary than they are.
explanation.direct: Procedure often launders vague purpose into legitimacy.
explanation.competitive: Booked is not the same as earned.

questions.prompt: Which of these fits the chapter's design logic?
choices: Use narrower attendance and written updates where live time adds little
Invite everyone because exclusion feels awkward
Keep every recurring meeting the same forever

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants live time reserved for what truly needs it.
explanation.direct: Attendance and async alternatives should answer to value.
explanation.competitive: Cut the room until necessity is what's left.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter mention written updates?
choices: Because some meeting goals can be handled asynchronously more efficiently
Because writing automatically replaces all live collaboration
Because meetings should never include information sharing

explanation.gentle: Some live time can be saved by moving updates out of the room.
explanation.direct: Async formats are part of good meeting design.
explanation.competitive: Not every status report deserves chairs.

questions.prompt: A recurring status meeting keeps taking an hour for eight people even though most updates are routine. What is the chapter's stronger correction?
choices: Move routine updates to writing and keep only the live discussion that truly requires the room
Make the meeting longer so people feel heard
Assume the time is justified because it is recurring

explanation.gentle: The meeting should shrink to the part that genuinely needs live discussion.
explanation.direct: The chapter would test the room against purpose and async alternatives.
explanation.competitive: Stop paying full price for low-value theater.

questions.prompt: What mistake does the chapter avoid by refusing a generic anti-meeting rant?
choices: Erasing the fact that some meetings really do deserve synchronous time
Assuming meetings can never improve
Treating calendars as unrelated to distraction

explanation.gentle: The chapter still allows useful meetings when they earn their time.
explanation.direct: It aims for earned meetings, not abolition.
explanation.competitive: Some rooms help. The lazy ones freeload.

questions.prompt: What practical levers help a meeting earn its claim?
choices: Agenda, narrower scope, smaller attendance, and shorter duration
Only louder facilitation
Keeping every participant on camera no matter what

explanation.gentle: The chapter relies on design discipline, not just energy.
explanation.direct: Sharper purpose and smaller claims are key meeting improvements.
explanation.competitive: A tighter room wastes less life.

questions.prompt: How does this chapter connect to the earlier chat and meeting-pressure material?
choices: It treats meetings as the larger synchronous time claims that can grow out of weak coordination norms
It abandons the communication theme entirely
It says meetings and chat are the exact same trigger source

explanation.gentle: The book is scaling from smaller interruptions to bigger calendar claims.
explanation.direct: Weak coordination norms can spill from chat into meetings.
explanation.competitive: Channel chaos often ends up renting a room.

questions.prompt: Why does the next chapter move into the smartphone?
choices: Because after shared time claims are tightened, the next portable trigger source is the device people carry everywhere
Because meetings are unrelated to external triggers
Because smartphones are only a workplace problem

explanation.gentle: The next trigger source is personal and portable rather than room-based.
explanation.direct: The section is shifting from organized claims on time to a device that follows the person everywhere.
explanation.competitive: Once the room stops stealing hours, the phone is still in your pocket.
